newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Industrial production/cap use.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Industrial production/cap use.

text.p: The economic data the U.S. Treasury market will sift through on Tuesday might provide some short-term trading opportunities but is not likely to push prices out of their current ranges, analysts said.
At 0915 EDT/1315 GMT, the Federal Reserve will release data on August industrial production and capacity use.
With manufacturing workweek data from the monthly U.S. payrolls report to guide them, economists estimate industrial production rose 0.4 percent in August.
Capacity use, the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in that production, is forecast at 83.3 percent.
Treasuries should take these data in stride, market analysts said.

"Unless something unusual happens, you generally get a pretty good picture of what the industrial production number will be from the payrolls data on the manufacturing sector," observed Richard Koss, economist at Maria Fiorini Ramirez Inc. "It doesn't come as a surprise."
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., looks for a 0.3 percent increase in August industrial production, with a 0.4 percent rise a possibility.

"A 0.3 percent industrial production rise would not signify "overwhelming strength, but it would tell us that the manufacturing sector is performing well," Moran said. "It leaves little doubt that the expansion is back on track."
Since the industrial production number is often accurately forecast, it is not likely to move the market, analysts said.
But a mild surprise to the upside could push yields higher, market analysts said.
The bellwether 30-year Treasury bond yield ended at 6.95 percent on Monday.

An industrial production rise of 0.5 percent might not move the 30-year bond yield above seven percent, but it would at least "impart a more negative tone to the market," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International.
An 83.3 reading on capacity utilization, meanwhile, would not raise inflation fears, economists said.
"We've been at higher (capacity use) levels in the past," Moran noted.
Second-tier data on department and chain-store sales could provide participants with some trading opportunities, market analysts said.
At 0900 EDT, the market gets the BTM/Schroders report on store sales in the latest week. And in mid-afternoon, the market gets the Lynch Jones & Ryan Redbook sales report.

"Unless the sales reflected in these reports start to pick up, we'll be showing consumption running at less than two percent in the third quarter which would be a decent drop from second-quarter consumption of 3.4 percent and first-quarter consumption of 3.5 percent," said Koss.

Koss said, however, that while the market could move a little bit on the store sales data, "they are not liable to change the picture" for a market that "at this point, has mostly priced out the notion of a (Federal Reserve) tightening next week."

Fed policy makers meet on September 24 and until last week's subdued reports on August inflation and retail sales, the market had expected the central bank to raise interest rates at that gathering. The very slight August inflation gains and only a 0.2 percent rise in August retail sales cast doubt over that conviction, however.
Dealers said they expect Federal funds to open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-5/16 percent on Tuesday.
